title: Relationships · Episode 3
chapters: Forgiveness: what it is, and what it isn't

units.t: Relationships. Episode three.
In this episode: Forgiveness: what it is, and what it isn't, Setting boundaries and Making friends as an adult.
Part one. Forgiveness: what it is, and what it isn't.
Forgiving someone does not mean forgetting, excusing or letting them back into your life.
Here is what forgiveness actually involves, and why researchers think it can lighten the load.
Setting the stone down.
Picture someone who, twenty years after a bitter family falling out, still replays the argument in the shower and feels their jaw tighten at the person's name.
The hurt took five minutes; the resentment has taken two decades.
Psychologists call this replaying rumination, and it keeps anger and distress fresh.
Forgiveness, in the research sense, is about gradually setting that stone down.
It does not mean saying what happened was acceptable, forgetting it, or trusting the person again.
Reconciliation, restoring a relationship, takes two people and requires the other to be safe and trustworthy.
Forgiveness can happen entirely inside one person, even if the other never apologises or has died.
You can forgive and still keep firm boundaries, report a crime or end a relationship.
Evidence and REACH.
People who forgive more readily generally report less anxiety, less depression and greater life satisfaction.
In experiments, people imagining a grudge showed bigger rises in heart rate and blood pressure than when imagining forgiving.
Structured programmes by Robert Enright and Everett Worthington have shown benefits in trials.
But much of the evidence is correlational: forgiving may make people healthier, or calmer people may forgive more easily.
Probably both.
Worthington's REACH approach has five steps.
Recall the hurt honestly.
Empathise, seeing the other person as a whole human without excusing them.
Give the altruistic gift of forgiveness, remembering times you were forgiven.
Commit, perhaps by writing a letter you never send.
Hold on, because old feelings resurface and that does not mean it failed.
Forgiveness on a national scale.
After apartheid ended, South Africa faced an enormous question: how could people who had suffered terrible abuses live alongside those responsible?
One answer was the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu in the late 1990s.
Victims could tell their stories publicly, and perpetrators could apply for amnesty if they fully disclosed politically motivated crimes.
Tutu championed the view that there is no future without forgiveness, the title of his book about the process.
The commission was praised worldwide and also criticised, with some victims feeling justice was sacrificed.
In Australia, the 2008 National Apology to the Stolen Generations showed how public acknowledgement of harm can matter deeply.
Forgiving yourself.
Sometimes the person we cannot forgive is ourselves.
Maybe you said something cruel to a parent before they died, or a mistake at work hurt others.
Researchers distinguish genuine self-forgiveness from simply excusing yourself.
Pseudo self-forgiveness skips responsibility: 'It wasn't really my fault.'
Genuine self-forgiveness starts by owning what you did, feeling appropriate remorse and making amends where possible, then releasing ongoing self-punishment.
This links to self-compassion, popularised by psychologist Kristin Neff: treating yourself with the kindness you would offer a friend who had made the same mistake.
Endless self-criticism rarely makes people better.
It more often makes them defensive, stuck or avoidant.
Accepting that you are a flawed human who can learn and repair is usually a better route to doing better.
Taking your time.
Forgiveness is not a switch you flick.
For serious harms it can take years, and some people decide not to forgive certain things, which is their right.
Pressuring someone to forgive, especially a person who has been abused, can add to their pain and even keep them in danger.
Safety and justice come first.
If you are experiencing abuse, 1800RESPECT, 1800 737 732, offers confidential support, and in an emergency call 000.
For everyday hurts, small steps help: noticing when you are rehearsing the grievance, wondering what was going on for the other person, and choosing to stop feeding the story.
This is general information, not therapy.
If an old hurt still dominates your life, a psychologist, counsellor or your GP can help.
Forgiving is ultimately something you do for your own freedom.
The key idea: Forgiveness means gradually releasing resentment, and it is not excusing, forgetting or reconciling.
Part two. Setting boundaries.
Boundaries aren't walls or ultimatums.
They're clear, kind statements about what you will and won't do.
What boundaries are.
A boundary is a limit you set for yourself: what you'll accept, how much time or energy you'll give, and what you'll share.
Healthy boundaries let you stay close to people without losing yourself.
They come in several kinds.
Physical boundaries cover personal space and touch.
Emotional boundaries mean not taking responsibility for other people's feelings.
Time boundaries might mean not answering work emails at night.
Material boundaries cover lending money or belongings.
They're like fences with gates you choose when to open.
A common mistake is trying to control others.
'You can't talk to me like that' is really a demand.
A boundary focuses on what you'll do: 'If you keep shouting, I'll leave the room and we can talk later.'
You can't make other people change, but you can decide how you respond.
Why they're hard.
People-pleasers often say yes when they mean no, then feel resentful, exhausted or quietly taken for granted.
Setting a boundary can trigger guilt, fear of conflict or fear of rejection.
Some people grew up in families where their needs weren't respected, so limits feel selfish or risky.
Without boundaries, people often burn out or quietly withdraw.
A clear boundary is often kinder than a reluctant yes.
Many people don't know their limits until they're crossed, but feelings are clues.
Resentment signals you're giving more than you want to.
Dread before seeing someone, or relief when plans are cancelled, may point to something needing attention.
Exhaustion can mean you're overextended.
Ask what is bothering you: the amount of time, the topic, or the way you're spoken to?
Saying it and holding it.
Effective boundaries are simple: 'I'm not able to take that on this week.'
'I need to leave by nine.'
Long justifications invite debate.
You can be warm and firm: 'I love seeing you, and I need you to call before coming over.'
Expect pushback, especially from people who benefited from your lack of boundaries.
Calm repetition works better than escalating.
You can also take time: 'Let me think about it and get back to you.'
A boundary only works with follow-through.
If you say you'll leave when someone shouts and then stay, people learn your limits are negotiable.
Follow-through needs no anger, just consistency.
Start with low-stakes boundaries, like not replying to non-urgent messages late at night.
Expect some discomfort, including guilt; it doesn't mean you've done something wrong.
Over time, people generally adjust.
Boundaries at work.
Work is one of the hardest places to set limits, especially when phones make everyone reachable at all hours.
In Australia, a 'right to disconnect' was added to the Fair Work Act, applying to most employers from August 2024 and to small businesses from August 2025.

It lets employees refuse to monitor, read or respond to work contact outside their working hours unless the refusal is unreasonable, taking into account things like their role, pay and the reason for the contact.
Beyond the law, practical steps help: agree on response times with your team, turn off notifications after hours, and negotiate priorities rather than silently absorbing extra work.
Respecting others' boundaries.
Boundaries go both ways.
When someone says no, accept it without pushing, sulking, guilt-tripping or punishing them later.
Notice if you react badly to other people's limits, and ask why: is it hurt, fear, or a sense of entitlement?
Respecting boundaries builds trust, because people feel safe being honest with you.
A relationship where one person's boundaries are consistently ignored, mocked or punished is a warning sign that may involve control or abuse.
In Australia, confidential support is available through 1800RESPECT, 1800 737 732, and anyone in immediate danger should call 000.
The key idea: A boundary is a limit on your own actions that protects what you'll accept, not a demand on someone else.
Part three. Making friends as an adult.
School gave us friends by default.
As adults, we have to make them on purpose.
Here's what works.
Why it gets harder.
At school and university, friendships formed almost automatically: you saw the same people daily and had free time.
Adult life scatters people through work, moves, relationships and children.
Many people make fewer new friends from their late twenties.
Surveys suggest many adults have fewer close friends than they'd like, and men in particular often report fewer people to confide in.
Friendship needs a more intentional approach, like fitness or a career.
Sociologists, including Rebecca Adams, describe three conditions for close friendship: proximity, repeated and unplanned interactions, and a setting that encourages people to confide.
School, team sports and share houses provide all three.
As an adult, you can recreate them by joining things that meet regularly, like a club, class, choir, volunteer group or sports team.
A single event doesn't give you repeated, casual encounters.
Show up and initiate.
Going to one event rarely creates a friend.
Going to the same weekly activity for months often does.
Familiarity builds trust, partly through the mere-exposure effect: we tend to like what's familiar.
Close friendships take many hours, so at a two-hour weekly activity, expect months, not weeks.
Pick something you'd enjoy anyway, and stay afterwards for a chat.
Many potential friendships stall because both people wait for the other to suggest something.
Be the initiator, and be specific about time and place, since 'we should catch up sometime' rarely happens.
Suggest something low-pressure, like a walk or coffee.
Don't read one declined invitation as rejection, since people's lives are full.
Try again, or suggest a different time.
Assume people like you.
Research on the 'acceptance prophecy', led by psychologist Danu Anthony Stinson, found that people who expect to be accepted act warmer and more open, which leads others to actually accept them.
Expecting rejection often makes people guarded, quiet or cold, which can create the rejection they fear.
Studies of the 'liking gap' by Erica Boothby and colleagues found that after a conversation, people consistently underestimated how much their new acquaintance liked them and enjoyed their company.
So assume the best and act accordingly: smile, ask questions and show interest.
Most people are privately worrying about the same things you are.
Old ties and change.
Some of the easiest friendships to grow are ones you already have.
In a 2011 study, Daniel Levin, Jorge Walter and Keith Murnighan asked executives to reconnect with contacts they hadn't spoken to for at least three years.
These ties often gave more valuable and novel advice than current ones, and people had worried more than necessary about awkwardness.
A simple message, like 'I was thinking of you the other day, how have you been?'
, is often enough.
Not every friendship lasts, and that isn't always failure.
A Dutch study by Gerald Mollenhorst found that over seven years, people kept only about half of their close network, with new people replacing those who drifted.
Friendships fade when circumstances change, and some can be revived.
Holding friendships a little loosely, with gratitude, makes room for new ones.
Deepening friendships.
Moving from casual to close friendship involves sharing more personal things gradually, being there in hard times, and creating shared memories, like a weekend away or a project together.
Remember details and follow up: 'How did the job interview go?'
Celebrate their good news genuinely.

Psychologist Shelly Gable found that responding to good news with enthusiasm and interest, which she called active-constructive responding, is linked to closer, more satisfying relationships, and may matter as much as support in bad times.
Keep contact going even when life is busy: a quick message, a shared joke or a standing monthly catch-up keeps a friendship alive between longer visits.
The key idea: Friendship grows from proximity, repeated unplanned contact and openness, which school provided and adult life scatters.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Which statement about forgiveness is true according to researchers?
Answer. It can happen without an apology.
Question two. Which is a well-phrased boundary?
Answer. If you keep shouting, I'll leave and we can talk later.
Question three. Which setting best matches the conditions for close friendship?
Answer. A weekly club or team with the same people.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
